open_obligations: Note that the doubly-efficient setting covers time-T computations, not all of PSPACE with an efficient honest prover.
Check that the oracle model of human judgement corresponds to Irving et al.'s polynomial-time judge H.
Check the role of O(S log T) verifier time when S is large.
in.other_title: Theorem 5.1: deterministic debate verifies time-T, space-S computations with O(1) queries
in.rationale: Irving et al.'s Theorem 1 shows polynomial-step debate with a polynomial-time judge decides PSPACE when debaters are unbounded. Brown-Cohen et al.'s Theorem 5.1 gives a bisection protocol (A states a middle configuration, B picks a half) deciding any time-T, space-S oracle computation with O(T log T) honest-prover time and O(1) oracle queries, restricting the honest prover to be efficient while the dishonest prover stays unbounded.
in.scope: proposed EXTENDS: recursive debate protocols for verifying long computations with few judge queries, from unbounded to polynomial-time honest provers

open_obligations: Note that Leike et al. state an informal analogy, not a theorem.
Check that the user's binary evaluation plays the role of Irving et al.'s polynomial-time judge H.
Check whether assistance agents answering subquestions map onto adversarial quantifiers.
in.other_title: Complexity analogy: reward modeling ~ NP, recursion depth k ~ k alternating quantifiers
in.rationale: Irving et al. show n-round debate with a polynomial-time judge corresponds to formulas with alternating quantifiers (Sigma_n P for fixed n, PSPACE with polynomially many rounds). Leike et al. credit this analogy to Irving et al. and argue reward modeling resembles NP while recursive reward modeling at depth k targets problems with k alternating quantifiers; no theorem is proved.
in.scope: proposed DEPENDS_ON: the complexity-theory analogy between recursion depth in oversight schemes and alternating quantifiers

text: The authors show that an n-round debate judged by a polynomial-time algorithm H corresponds to formulas of the form 'exists x0 for all x1 ... H(q, x0, ...)', giving the class Sigma_n P for fixed n and PSPACE when the number of rounds grows polynomially in the question size. Theorem 1 states that for any problem L in PSPACE a polynomial-time judge can be chosen so that optimal play in a debate with polynomially many steps solves L.
title: Theorem 1: debate with a polynomial-time judge and optimal play decides PSPACE
